screens.title: Introduction to ROS Actions and Actionlib
screens.narratorSegment: Actions in ROS let your robot perform multi-second tasks while still remaining responsive. In this lesson you will learn what an action is, why you choose it instead of a service, and the pieces that make the action protocol work: a goal, periodic feedback, a final result, and the ability to cancel or preempt a running task. We will study a small, concrete example — a CountUntil action that counts from one to a target number — and implement both the server and client in Python. You will see how actionlib hides the low-level topics and gives you a simple A P I for sending goals, receiving feedback, and canceling work. Along the way we will cover common pitfalls: blocking clients, failing to honor preemption requests, and mixing up feedback with results. By the end of the chapter you will be able to choose between services, topics, and actions for common robot tasks and implement a SimpleActionServer and SimpleActionClient. Think about a simple long-running operation on your robot now — a movement, a survey scan, or a timed task — and keep that in mind as we build the server and client. Which parts will need feedback, and when might you want to cancel the operation?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Actions give you asynchronous, cancellable tasks with live feedback — ideal for motion, long computations, and any operation that needs progress updates or cancellation.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Intro to Actions
Actions vs Services: a practical lens
When tasks take time and you need status or cancellation, actions are the right tool.
Asynchronous progress
Actions stream feedback while running long tasks.
Cancelable work
Clients can request preemption to stop the server mid-task.
Actionlib handles topics
You interact via a high-level API; actionlib manages goal/status/feedback topics.
Explore Key Topics
Action protocol
Goal, periodic feedback, result, and preemption for long tasks.
Server & Client
SimpleActionServer runs the job; SimpleActionClient sends goals and receives updates.
When to use
Choose actions for motion and anything needing progress or cancellation.
Visual Concept
Client
Sends a goal, listens for feedback, and can cancel.
Example: request to count to 10. Receive progress updates and optionally cancel.
Server
Accepts goals and publishes feedback and final result. Honors preemption.
Example: a counting loop that publishes percent complete and sets succeeded or preempted.
In this lesson
You will read .action files, implement a Python server and client, and run a short hands-on activity to practice cancellation and feedback behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will develop four core competencies. First, you will explain why actions are needed for long-running tasks that services cannot handle. A clear example is moving an arm to a position: the client should not block, and must be able to cancel mid-motion. Second, you will understand the action protocol: the goal a client sends, the periodic feedback the server streams, the final result, and how preemption works. Knowing these pieces helps you design safe, cancellable tasks. Third, you will implement a SimpleActionServer in Python that processes goals, publishes feedback during execution, and returns a result or preempts when requested. This includes handling rate loops, checking is_preempt_requested, and calling set_succeeded or set_preempted. Fourth, you will implement a SimpleActionClient in Python that sends goals, receives feedback callbacks, handles done callbacks, waits for the server, and cancels goals. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a demonstration task so you can verify your progress. These skills let you pick the right communication primitive in ROS and create responsive robot behaviors. As you work through examples, compare each pattern to a service call to reinforce when actions are the correct choice.

screens.title: Why actions instead of services?
screens.narratorSegment: Services are simple request-response pairs that work well for quick checks and short commands, but they are synchronous and block the client until completion. Imagine asking a service to move a robotic arm to a target and waiting five seconds; the client cannot do anything else until the service returns. Actions address this by decoupling request and execution. An action client sends a goal and immediately regains control, while the server processes the task and streams feedback. This matters because robots must often react while a long operation runs — for example, stopping motion when an obstacle appears. A common misconception is to use services for simplicity and only later refactor to actions; this can lead to brittle systems where critical cancellation is difficult to retrofit. In practice, prefer services for atomic, fast checks like reading a battery level or toggling an LED. Use topics for streaming telemetry without explicit completion semantics. Use actions when you need a clearly bounded operation, progress updates, and cancellation. A concrete example: a drone takeoff sequence needs altitude feedback and the ability to abort; this is an action, not a service. Key takeaway: match the communication primitive to the task duration, progress requirements, and cancellation needs.

keyIdea.title: When to choose actions
keyIdea.text: If a task can take multiple seconds and requires progress updates or cancellation, pick actions instead of services or plain topics.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Compare Primitives
Service (synchronous)
Best for quick, atomic requests.
  • Request-response pattern.
  • Blocks client until completion.
  • No standard cancellation or progress stream.
Common mistake
Using a service for long-running movement. The client will block and cannot cancel mid-way.
Action (asynchronous)
For long-running tasks that need feedback and cancellation.
  • Client sends a goal and continues immediately.
  • Server publishes feedback periodically and a final result.
  • Client can request preemption to cancel the goal.
Key takeaway
Use actions when progress reporting and cancellation are required for safety or responsiveness.

screens.title: Action protocol: goal, feedback, result, preemption
screens.narratorSegment: An action follows a simple, repeatable protocol that supports asynchronous execution and control. First, the client sends a goal that describes the requested work, for example a target position or a maximum count. The server accepts the goal and moves the task into an active state. While the task runs, the server publishes feedback at regular intervals so the client can observe progress — feedback might be percent complete or the robot's current pose. When the task finishes, the server sends a result that contains the final outcome. Crucially, the client can request preemption at any time. When the server detects a preemption request, it should stop the task cleanly, set the goal as preempted, and return an appropriate status. A concrete example from the chapter is CountUntil: the client sends max_number as the goal, the server publishes percentage feedback during the loop, and returns the final count as the result. A common misconception is that feedback is the same as a result; it is not — feedback is transient progress, result is final. Key takeaway: design your goal, feedback, and result fields to give enough information for the client to make decisions and for the server to report meaningful progress.

keyIdea.title: Protocol structure
keyIdea.text: Goal starts the work, feedback reports progress, result finalizes the outcome, and preemption allows cancellation.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Action Protocol
Timeline
1. Goal
Request describing the task, e.g., max_number or target pose.
2. Active
Server accepts and runs the task.
3. Feedback
Periodic updates such as percentage or current pose.
4. Result
Final outcome: success flag, count, or message.
Preemption
Client may request cancel; server should stop and set preempted.
Example: CountUntil.action
# File: action/CountUntil.action
# Goal
int32 max_number
---
# Result
int32 count
---
# Feedback
float32 percentage
This action sends max_number as the goal, streams percentage feedback, and returns the final count as the result. Design fields so feedback answers progress questions the client will ask.

screens.title: Defining a custom .action file
screens.narratorSegment: Custom actions are defined in. action files and placed in your package's action directory. Each. action file has three sections separated by three hyphens: the goal, the result, and the feedback. The goal section contains the fields the client will send, such as an integer max_number or a target pose. The result contains values the server returns once finished, and feedback holds transient status updates. After creating the. action file, you must add it to CMakeLists. txt with add_action_files and include actionlib_msgs and message_generation in dependencies. Then call generate_messages with the required dependencies and add actionlib_msgs to package. xml as build and exec dependencies. A common mistake is to forget generate_messages or to misplace the file; if messages are not built, the Python imports for CountUntilAction and related generated types will fail. Concrete example: CountUntil. action declares int32 max_number, int32 count, and float32 percentage. Build steps in CMakeLists. txt and package. xml make these types available when you build the package. Takeaway: the. action file is small but essential; ensure it is listed for generation and your package declares the right dependencies so the generated message types are available in Python or C++.

Module 4›Chapter 4.1›.action files
File structure
# File: action/CountUntil.action
# Goal
int32 max_number
---
# Result
int32 count
---
# Feedback
float32 percentage
Three sections are required and the separators must be exactly three hyphens. Choose field names and types that give clients the right control and servers the right reporting information.
Build integration
find_package(catkin REQUIRED COMPONENTS
  actionlib_msgs
  message_generation
)

add_action_files(
  FILES
  CountUntil.action
)

generate_messages(
  DEPENDENCIES
  std_msgs
  actionlib_msgs
)
Also add actionlib_msgs as build and exec dependencies in package.xml so generated headers and Python modules are available to your nodes.

screens.title: SimpleActionServer in Python
screens.narratorSegment: The SimpleActionServer is your server-side worker that implements the action protocol for each goal. In Python you create a SimpleActionServer with the action type and an execute callback. The execute callback runs in a separate thread and should perform the long-running work. Inside the callback, publish feedback periodically with publish_feedback and check is_preempt_requested to gracefully stop if the client cancels. When work completes normally, call set_succeeded with a result object; if canceled, call set_preempted. A concrete server implementation from the chapter is CountUntilServer: it starts the server, logs the goal, and loops from one to max_number at 2 Hz. On each iteration it constructs CountUntilFeedback with percentage set to i divided by max_number and calls publish_feedback. If is_preempt_requested returns true the server logs, calls set_preempted, and breaks the loop. Finally, if success remains true, it populates CountUntilResult and calls set_succeeded. A common pitfall is forgetting to call start() when auto_start=False, or failing to call set_preempted when canceling; this leaves clients waiting or misreports state. Practice: run the server locally and insert deliberate preemption requests from a client to observe correct transitions.

keyIdea.title: Server responsibilities
keyIdea.text: Run the work in execute_cb, publish feedback, check for preemption, and set succeeded or preempted with the appropriate result.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Action Server
Server core pattern
import rospy
import actionlib
from my_first_robot.msg import CountUntilAction, CountUntilFeedback, CountUntilResult

class CountUntilServer:
    def __init__(self):
        self._as = actionlib.SimpleActionServer('/count_until', CountUntilAction,
            execute_cb=self.execute_callback, auto_start=False)
        self._as.start()

    def execute_callback(self, goal):
        success = True
        rate = rospy.Rate(2)
        for i in range(1, goal.max_number + 1):
            if self._as.is_preempt_requested():
                self._as.set_preempted()
                success = False
                break
            feedback = CountUntilFeedback()
            feedback.percentage = float(i) / float(goal.max_number)
            self._as.publish_feedback(feedback)
            rate.sleep()
        if success:
            result = CountUntilResult()
            result.count = goal.max_number
            self._as.set_succeeded(result)
Keep loops responsive and check preemption frequently. Use a reasonable feedback rate so the client sees smooth progress without overwhelming the network.
Explanation and tips
  • auto_start=False prevents the server from handling goals before initialization; call start() after setup.
  • execute_cb runs on its own thread; avoid blocking other ROS operations without care.
  • Call publish_feedback often and set_succeeded or set_preempted exactly once per goal.
Developer note
Design result types to capture success and diagnostic info so clients can decide next steps.

screens.title: SimpleActionClient in Python
screens.narratorSegment: The SimpleActionClient provides the manager-side A P I to interact with action servers. In Python you create a SimpleActionClient for a named action and call wait_for_server to ensure the server is available. You build a goal message, send it with send_goal, and optionally supply feedback and done callbacks to handle asynchronous updates. The feedback callback receives periodic feedback messages so your application can react to progress. The done callback receives status and result once the action completes; status codes indicate pending, active, preempted, succeeded, or aborted. You can cancel a running goal with cancel_goal to request preemption. A concrete client example is CountUntilClient: it waits for the server, sends a CountUntilGoal with max_number set, logs feedback percent in feedback_callback, cancels after a delay to trigger preemption, and inspects the done_callback to log final status. A subtle point is that cancel_goal is a request; if the server already set succeeded the cancel has no effect. Practice listening to feedback and writing robust done handlers that handle preempted and succeeded states gracefully. SimpleActionClient in Python means wait for the server, send goals, process feedback updates, handle the done callback, and use cancel_goal to request preemption.. In practical terms, sending goals, receiving feedback, handling done and cancellation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Action Client
Client code pattern
import rospy
import actionlib
from my_first_robot.msg import CountUntilAction, CountUntilGoal

class CountUntilClient:
    def __init__(self):
        self._ac = actionlib.SimpleActionClient('/count_until', CountUntilAction)
        self._ac.wait_for_server()

    def send_goal(self, max_number):
        goal = CountUntilGoal()
        goal.max_number = max_number
        self._ac.send_goal(goal, done_cb=self.done_callback, feedback_cb=self.feedback_callback)

    def feedback_callback(self, feedback):
        rospy.loginfo("Feedback: %.1f%%", feedback.percentage * 100)

    def done_callback(self, status, result):
        rospy.loginfo("Done! Status: %d, Count: %d", status, result.count)

    def cancel(self):
        self._ac.cancel_goal()
Ensure your callbacks are non-blocking and handle all expected status codes to avoid race conditions between cancel requests and server completion.
Practical notes
  • wait_for_server blocks until a server is available; use it during startup to avoid lost goals.
  • Feedback callbacks help update UI or decision logic while the action runs.
  • Check action status codes in done callbacks to respond to preemption or errors.
Try this
Send a goal then call cancel after two seconds. Observe PREEMPTED in the done callback.

screens.title: Action states and transitions
screens.narratorSegment: Actionlib defines a set of standard states that describe the lifecycle of a goal. PENDING means the goal was sent but not yet started; ACTIVE means the server is currently processing it. PREEMPTED indicates the client requested cancellation and the server acknowledged and stopped the task. SUCCEEDED means the server completed the work successfully and returned a result. ABORTED means the server stopped due to an internal error or inability to complete the goal. REJECTED is used when the server refuses to accept the goal at all, for example if parameters are invalid. A concrete example: the client sends a goal and sees PENDING while the server prepares; once the server accepts it, status becomes ACTIVE and feedback pulses arrive. If the client calls cancel_goal while the server is still running, you should see PREEMPTED if the server honors the request. Misunderstanding these states leads to incorrect client behavior — for instance, attempting to cancel after the server already set succeeded has no effect. The key design principle is to monitor status transitions and write done callbacks that differentiate preempted from succeeded and aborted outcomes so your application can react appropriately.

narration.text: Actionlib defines a set of standard states that describe the lifecycle of a goal. PENDING means the goal was sent but not yet started; ACTIVE means the server is currently processing it. PREEMPTED indicates the client requested cancellation and the server acknowledged and stopped the task. SUCCEEDED means the server completed the work successfully and returned a result. ABORTED means the server stopped due to an internal error or inability to complete the goal. REJECTED is used when the server refuses to accept the goal at all, for example if parameters are invalid. A concrete example: the client sends a goal and sees PENDING while the server prepares; once the server accepts it, status becomes ACTIVE and feedback pulses arrive. If the client calls cancel_goal while the server is still running, you should see PREEMPTED if the server honors the request. Misunderstanding these states leads to incorrect client behavior — for instance, attempting to cancel after the server already set succeeded has no effect. The key design principle is to monitor status transitions and write done callbacks that differentiate preempted from succeeded and aborted outcomes so your application can react appropriately.

keyIdea.title: State machine
keyIdea.text: Track action states to reason about progress and to handle success, cancellation, or failures reliably in client code.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Action States
PENDING (1)
Goal sent but not yet started.
ACTIVE (2)
Server processing and publishing feedback.
PREEMPTED (3)
Client requested cancel and server stopped the goal.
SUCCEEDED (4)
Task completed successfully; result returned.
ABORTED (5)
Server aborted due to an internal error or inability to proceed.
REJECTED (6)
Server refused the goal before starting, often due to validation.
Practical test
Send a goal, cancel it mid-execution, and observe PREEMPTED in the done callback. Then send another goal and let it complete to observe SUCCEEDED.

screens.title: Actionlib internals and hidden topics
screens.narratorSegment: Actionlib hides a set of internal topics and messages that implement the action protocol. Behind the SimpleActionServer and SimpleActionClient are topics for goals, cancellations, feedback, status, and results. The advantage for you is a simple A P I; the disadvantage is that you must understand the contract if you debug connectivity or inspect rqt_graph. A practical example is that an action appears in rqt_graph as multiple topics: goal, cancel, status, feedback, and result endpoints. This split allows the server and client to communicate asynchronously without single-thread blocking. When troubleshooting, verify the server node is advertising the action and that both client and server share the same action type and name. A common misconception is that actionlib is a single topic — it is not; it uses multiple channels to keep state and messages decoupled. For safe design, keep feedback messages small and frequent enough for responsive UIs, and ensure result messages carry any diagnostic text to explain SUCCEEDED or ABORTED outcomes. Understanding these internals helps when you need to visualize communication with rqt_graph or diagnose missed messages in noisy networks.

keyIdea.title: Internal plumbing
keyIdea.text: Actionlib uses multiple hidden topics for goal, cancel, status, feedback, and result; the high-level API abstracts this but knowing it helps debugging.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Actionlib internals
Hidden channels managed by actionlib
Goal / Cancel
Goals and cancel requests travel over separate topics so the client can signal preemption at any time.
Feedback / Result
Feedback is streamed frequently; the final result is published once when the goal completes.
Status
A status topic provides goal state information so clients and monitors can track active goals.
Debug tip
Use rqt_graph to view the multiple topics an action creates; this reveals why actions show several connections rather than a single line.
Practical note
When debugging, confirm action names and types match exactly and that message generation completed so the nodes can import the generated types.

screens.title: Hands-on: Build MoveRobot.action and simulate motion
screens.narratorSegment: In this hands-on activity you will define a MoveRobot. action and implement server and client nodes that simulate motion over five seconds with feedback every half second. The action's goal contains a geometry_msgs/Pose target_pose; the feedback includes the current_pose and a float progress between 0.0 and 1.0; the result returns a boolean success and a message string. Implement the server so it interpolates from the current pose to the target over ten steps, publishing feedback each step and sleeping 0.5 seconds. Regularly check is_preempt_requested and if true call set_preempted and stop. Implement the client to send a goal for target pose (5,5), subscribe to feedback to print progress, then call cancel_goal after two seconds to test preemption. Run both nodes and observe action states in the terminal: PENDING, ACTIVE, PREEMPTED. Then modify the client to not cancel and observe SUCCEEDED. A frequent mistake is failing to import geometry_msgs when declaring the action or forgetting to list MoveRobot. action for generation. The learning objective here is to combine message design, server-side loop control, and client cancellation to see state transitions in practice.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Design a MoveRobot action, simulate timed movement with feedback, and verify preemption when the client cancels mid-motion.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Hands-on
MoveRobot.action example
# MoveRobot.action
geometry_msgs/Pose target_pose
---
bool success
string message
---
geometry_msgs/Pose current_pose
float32 progress
Declare this file in action/ and add it to add_action_files so the types are generated. Use geometry_msgs types in CMake and package.xml dependencies.
Server behavior checklist
  • Interpolate pose over 10 steps, publish feedback every 0.5s.
  • Check is_preempt_requested each loop and set_preempted when cancelled.
  • On success, set_succeeded with success=true and a descriptive message.
Run the server and client together and watch terminal logs for status transitions and feedback lines printing progress.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: When working with actions, several recurring issues can cause frustration. First, missing message generation: if you forget to list your. action file in CMakeLists. txt or forget generate_messages, imports for CountUntilAction and related types will fail. Second, mismatched action names or types: client and server must use the same action name and generated type or they will not connect. Third, forgetting to call start() on the server when auto_start=False prevents it from accepting goals. Fourth, not checking is_preempt_requested often enough leaves the server slow to respond to cancellation. For debugging, inspect rqt_graph to see the multiple topics an action creates and confirm both nodes appear. Use rosnode list and rostopic echo on feedback and result topics to observe live messages. Log descriptive messages when calling set_succeeded, set_preempted, or set_aborted so terminals reflect why a goal ended. A subtle race condition occurs if the client calls cancel_goal after the server already set succeeded; the cancel has no effect and the client should handle the succeeded result. The takeaway is to verify message generation and naming first, then check server start and loop responsiveness, and finally watch topic traffic with rqt_graph or rostopic to pinpoint where messages are lost.

keyIdea.title: Debugging checklist
keyIdea.text: Verify message generation, matching action names/types, server start, loop preemption checks, and observe topics with rqt_graph or rostopic.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Debugging
Message generation
If imports fail, rebuild and verify add_action_files and generate_messages were used.
Name/type mismatch
Client and server must use the same action name and generated types to connect.
Preemption checks
Poll is_preempt_requested frequently; a long sleep without checks delays cancellation handling.
Server start
Remember start() when using auto_start=False; otherwise the server will not accept goals.
Use logs
Log when you set_succeeded, set_preempted, or set_aborted to make terminal output diagnostic.
Observe topics
Use rqt_graph and rostopic echo on feedback and result topics to see live messages.

screens.title: Assessment scenario and reflection
screens.narratorSegment: Use the provided assessment scenario to test your understanding. A drone needs to take off, hover at ten meters, and then land. The client must monitor altitude and be able to abort takeoff if a problem occurs. Should this be implemented as a service or an action? The correct choice is an action. Actions support long-running operations, provide feedback such as altitude updates, and allow the client to cancel during takeoff if sensors detect an anomaly. When designing the action, include target altitude in the goal, the current altitude and a progress float in feedback, and a boolean success plus a text message in the result. A common misconception is that a service could be 'fast enough' — but takeoff spans multiple seconds and needs continuous monitoring and potential cancellation. For assessment, outline the goal, feedback, and result fields for the drone, implement mock server and client that simulate altitude changes, and demonstrate canceling during ascent. Conclude by explaining why a service would block monitoring logic and how using an action improves safety and responsiveness for this flight scenario. Assessment scenario and reflection means long operations that require monitoring and cancellation — like drone takeoff — should use actions to support progress reporting and safe aborts.. In practical terms, choosing actions: a drone takeoff and abort use case. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Assessment
Scenario: drone takeoff
Suggested Goal
target_altitude (float) and an identifier for the flight.
Suggested Feedback
current_altitude (float) and progress (0.0–1.0) published frequently during ascent.
Suggested Result
success (bool) and message (string) describing completion or failure reason.
Why not a service?
A service would block the client and provide no continuous altitude updates or safe mid-flight cancellation.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the three core ideas you should carry forward. First: actions are designed for long-running, asynchronous tasks where progress updates and cancellation are essential. Use them for motion, timed operations, and tasks that must be interruptible. Second: the action protocol is goal, feedback, result, and preemption. Design these fields intentionally so clients can monitor progress and choose when to cancel or retry. Third: actionlib simplifies interaction by exposing a server and client A P I, but it uses multiple underlying topics. If you debug connectivity, inspect rqt_graph and verify message generation and matching action names. As a quick reflection, name one long-running operation on your robot that needs mid-run cancellation and feedback. That operation is likely a good candidate for an action rather than a service. Key Concepts means actions = asynchronous + feedback + preemption; design .action files carefully; use actionlib but know the underlying topics for debugging.. In practical terms, three essential ideas from this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4›Chapter 4.1›Quick Reference
.action file
Three sections: goal, result, feedback. Add to add_action_files and generate messages.
Server
Run execute_cb, publish feedback, honor preemption, and set final state.
Client
Wait for server, send goals, handle feedback and done callbacks, and cancel when needed.
Closing question

Which long-running robot task will you convert to an action first, and what feedback will your server publish to make it safe?

fullNarratorScript:
Actions in ROS let your robot perform multi-second tasks while still remaining responsive. In this lesson you will learn what an action is, why you choose it instead of a service, and the pieces that make the action protocol work: a goal, periodic feedback, a final result, and the ability to cancel or preempt a running task. We will study a small, concrete example — a CountUntil action that counts from one to a target number — and implement both the server and client in Python. You will see how actionlib hides the low-level topics and gives you a simple A P I for sending goals, receiving feedback, and canceling work. Along the way we will cover common pitfalls: blocking clients, failing to honor preemption requests, and mixing up feedback with results. By the end of the chapter you will be able to choose between services, topics, and actions for common robot tasks and implement a SimpleActionServer and SimpleActionClient. Think about a simple long-running operation on your robot now — a movement, a survey scan, or a timed task — and keep that in mind as we build the server and client. Which parts will need feedback, and when might you want to cancel the operation?

In this chapter you will develop four core competencies. First, you will explain why actions are needed for long-running tasks that services cannot handle. A clear example is moving an arm to a position: the client should not block, and must be able to cancel mid-motion. Second, you will understand the action protocol: the goal a client sends, the periodic feedback the server streams, the final result, and how preemption works. Knowing these pieces helps you design safe, cancellable tasks. Third, you will implement a SimpleActionServer in Python that processes goals, publishes feedback during execution, and returns a result or preempts when requested. This includes handling rate loops, checking is_preempt_requested, and calling set_succeeded or set_preempted. Fourth, you will implement a SimpleActionClient in Python that sends goals, receives feedback callbacks, handles done callbacks, waits for the server, and cancels goals. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a demonstration task so you can verify your progress. These skills let you pick the right communication primitive in ROS and create responsive robot behaviors. As you work through examples, compare each pattern to a service call to reinforce when actions are the correct choice.

This second objectives slide explains how you will practice each skill and what to check for. For explaining why actions are needed, you will compare a short service-based request to an action-based counting task. Verify understanding by describing what would block a client and why cancellation is required. For the protocol, you will trace a timeline: goal sent, server active, feedback pulses, and result returned. As you trace it, watch for where cancellation can be requested. For the server implementation, you will run the CountUntil server, observe periodic feedback at a fixed rate, deliberately request preemption, and confirm the server sets preempted. For the client, you will send a goal, log feedback updates, and call cancel after a delay to observe PREEMPTED state. Each exercise ends with a milestone: a running demo that shows feedback and the expected action state transitions. This practice-focused view helps you move from concept to code and allows a reproducible check to confirm you implemented preemption and feedback correctly.

Services are simple request-response pairs that work well for quick checks and short commands, but they are synchronous and block the client until completion. Imagine asking a service to move a robotic arm to a target and waiting five seconds; the client cannot do anything else until the service returns. Actions address this by decoupling request and execution. An action client sends a goal and immediately regains control, while the server processes the task and streams feedback. This matters because robots must often react while a long operation runs — for example, stopping motion when an obstacle appears. A common misconception is to use services for simplicity and only later refactor to actions; this can lead to brittle systems where critical cancellation is difficult to retrofit. In practice, prefer services for atomic, fast checks like reading a battery level or toggling an LED. Use topics for streaming telemetry without explicit completion semantics. Use actions when you need a clearly bounded operation, progress updates, and cancellation. A concrete example: a drone takeoff sequence needs altitude feedback and the ability to abort; this is an action, not a service. Key takeaway: match the communication primitive to the task duration, progress requirements, and cancellation needs.

An action follows a simple, repeatable protocol that supports asynchronous execution and control. First, the client sends a goal that describes the requested work, for example a target position or a maximum count. The server accepts the goal and moves the task into an active state. While the task runs, the server publishes feedback at regular intervals so the client can observe progress — feedback might be percent complete or the robot's current pose. When the task finishes, the server sends a result that contains the final outcome. Crucially, the client can request preemption at any time. When the server detects a preemption request, it should stop the task cleanly, set the goal as preempted, and return an appropriate status. A concrete example from the chapter is CountUntil: the client sends max_number as the goal, the server publishes percentage feedback during the loop, and returns the final count as the result. A common misconception is that feedback is the same as a result; it is not — feedback is transient progress, result is final. Key takeaway: design your goal, feedback, and result fields to give enough information for the client to make decisions and for the server to report meaningful progress.

Custom actions are defined in. action files and placed in your package's action directory. Each. action file has three sections separated by three hyphens: the goal, the result, and the feedback. The goal section contains the fields the client will send, such as an integer max_number or a target pose. The result contains values the server returns once finished, and feedback holds transient status updates. After creating the. action file, you must add it to CMakeLists. txt with add_action_files and include actionlib_msgs and message_generation in dependencies. Then call generate_messages with the required dependencies and add actionlib_msgs to package. xml as build and exec dependencies. A common mistake is to forget generate_messages or to misplace the file; if messages are not built, the Python imports for CountUntilAction and related generated types will fail. Concrete example: CountUntil. action declares int32 max_number, int32 count, and float32 percentage. Build steps in CMakeLists. txt and package. xml make these types available when you build the package. Takeaway: the. action file is small but essential; ensure it is listed for generation and your package declares the right dependencies so the generated message types are available in Python or C++.

The SimpleActionServer is your server-side worker that implements the action protocol for each goal. In Python you create a SimpleActionServer with the action type and an execute callback. The execute callback runs in a separate thread and should perform the long-running work. Inside the callback, publish feedback periodically with publish_feedback and check is_preempt_requested to gracefully stop if the client cancels. When work completes normally, call set_succeeded with a result object; if canceled, call set_preempted. A concrete server implementation from the chapter is CountUntilServer: it starts the server, logs the goal, and loops from one to max_number at 2 Hz. On each iteration it constructs CountUntilFeedback with percentage set to i divided by max_number and calls publish_feedback. If is_preempt_requested returns true the server logs, calls set_preempted, and breaks the loop. Finally, if success remains true, it populates CountUntilResult and calls set_succeeded. A common pitfall is forgetting to call start() when auto_start=False, or failing to call set_preempted when canceling; this leaves clients waiting or misreports state. Practice: run the server locally and insert deliberate preemption requests from a client to observe correct transitions.

The SimpleActionClient provides the manager-side A P I to interact with action servers. In Python you create a SimpleActionClient for a named action and call wait_for_server to ensure the server is available. You build a goal message, send it with send_goal, and optionally supply feedback and done callbacks to handle asynchronous updates. The feedback callback receives periodic feedback messages so your application can react to progress. The done callback receives status and result once the action completes; status codes indicate pending, active, preempted, succeeded, or aborted. You can cancel a running goal with cancel_goal to request preemption. A concrete client example is CountUntilClient: it waits for the server, sends a CountUntilGoal with max_number set, logs feedback percent in feedback_callback, cancels after a delay to trigger preemption, and inspects the done_callback to log final status. A subtle point is that cancel_goal is a request; if the server already set succeeded the cancel has no effect. Practice listening to feedback and writing robust done handlers that handle preempted and succeeded states gracefully. SimpleActionClient in Python means wait for the server, send goals, process feedback updates, handle the done callback, and use cancel_goal to request preemption.. In practical terms, sending goals, receiving feedback, handling done and cancellation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Actionlib defines a set of standard states that describe the lifecycle of a goal. PENDING means the goal was sent but not yet started; ACTIVE means the server is currently processing it. PREEMPTED indicates the client requested cancellation and the server acknowledged and stopped the task. SUCCEEDED means the server completed the work successfully and returned a result. ABORTED means the server stopped due to an internal error or inability to complete the goal. REJECTED is used when the server refuses to accept the goal at all, for example if parameters are invalid. A concrete example: the client sends a goal and sees PENDING while the server prepares; once the server accepts it, status becomes ACTIVE and feedback pulses arrive. If the client calls cancel_goal while the server is still running, you should see PREEMPTED if the server honors the request. Misunderstanding these states leads to incorrect client behavior — for instance, attempting to cancel after the server already set succeeded has no effect. The key design principle is to monitor status transitions and write done callbacks that differentiate preempted from succeeded and aborted outcomes so your application can react appropriately.
